analysis.one_liner: Requires electric suppliers to steadily raise the share of power they get from renewables.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee in June 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every company that sells electricity to retail customers to increase the share of power it gets from renewable sources — starting at 1.5% in 2020 and rising through 2035. Suppliers could meet the requirement by earning, buying, or borrowing federal renewable energy credits, or by paying a fee capped at 3 cents per kilowatt-hour. The Energy Department would run a credit-tracking system, and fees collected would fund state grants for renewable energy and for energy assistance and weatherization for low-income households. It never got past the committee it was referred to.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, renewable energy developers and equipment makers would have gained a guaranteed, growing market for wind, solar, geothermal, and other renewable power. Communities hit by coal mine or coal plant closures and projects on Indian land would have earned double credits. Low-income households would have gotten weatherization and energy assistance funded by supplier fees. Everyone would share in cleaner air and lower climate emissions as fossil generation was displaced.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renewable energy builders and low-income households

how_it_helps.text: Each retail electric supplier would have to show, through credits submitted to the Energy Department, that its electricity sales met a rising renewable percentage each year from 2020 through 2035.

Projects located on Indian land or in economically distressed communities affected by coal mine or coal plant closures would earn two renewable energy credits for each kilowatt-hour generated instead of one.

Fees paid by suppliers in lieu of credits would go into a state renewable energy account used for grants to promote renewable production and to provide energy assistance and weatherization services to low-income consumers.

The bill's findings state that renewable energy is already the cheapest new form of electricity in many regions, and that meeting U.S. climate goals requires every state to transition to carbon-free electricity by 2050.

analysis.who_pays: Retail electric suppliers — mainly utilities and power companies — would bear the cost of buying credits or building renewable capacity. The bill guarantees rate-regulated utilities the ability to recover their prudently incurred incremental compliance costs, so much of that cost would likely flow to electricity customers through rates. Fossil generators, especially coal plants, would lose market share as suppliers shifted to renewables.
analysis.who_pays_short: Utilities, and likely electricity customers through rates

drawbacks.text: The bill lets rate-regulated utilities recover their full prudently incurred incremental cost of complying, so compliance costs would likely be passed on to electricity customers through their bills.

A supplier that did not want to build or buy renewables could instead make an alternative compliance payment capped at the lesser of 3 cents per kilowatt-hour or 200 percent of the market value of credits, a price ceiling critics could argue is cheap enough to let suppliers pay rather than build.

The bill counts biomass — including logging residues and mill byproducts — and incremental hydropower upgrades as qualifying renewable resources, categories that carry their own environmental debates even though the bill subjects hydropower to existing environmental licensing laws.
States that already get more than 60 percent of their electricity from renewables, or that run a stronger program of their own, could opt out of the federal requirement entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would create a steady national market for renewable electricity with real public benefits in air quality and climate, plus targeted help for coal-affected communities and low-income households through double credits and weatherization grants. The honest trade-off is that compliance costs would largely show up on electric bills, softened by the fact that the bill's own findings note renewables are often the cheapest new power source, and by flexibility features (credit trading, borrowing, a low fee cap) that lower the bill but also lower how much renewable capacity actually gets built. It was a moderate, incremental standard rather than a rapid decarbonization mandate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2019 and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never took it up; when the Congress ended in January 2021 the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Udall introduced the Renewable Electricity Standard Act in the Senate on June 26, 2019.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
Six senators cosponsored the bill — five Democrats and one independent.
The action history shows no further congressional action after the referral; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The electric utilities and fossil generators that would have had to buy renewable credits or build renewable capacity are better off that the bill died, since they avoided a federal compliance obligation. Working people forwent the cleaner air, climate benefits, and low-income weatherization funding it would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities that avoided a renewable mandate

against.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors were Democrats or independents, no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired Energy Committee never moved the bill; no roll-call votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: Renewable energy developers and equipment makers
industries.note: The standard would create a guaranteed, growing national market for new wind, solar, geothermal, and other renewable generation, with federal credits issued and tracked by the Energy Department. Cheaper clean power and cleaner air would flow to the public alongside the industry's gains.

industries.industry: Coal-fired and other fossil power generation
industries.note: As suppliers were required to shift their mix toward renewables, fossil generators would lose sales and eventually face retirement pressure. The bill softened the blow for coal communities by granting double credits for renewable projects in areas hit by coal mine or coal plant closures.

Utilities would bear the compliance burden but got flexibility — credit trading, borrowing against future credits, a low alternative compliance fee — and a guarantee they could recover prudent compliance costs from ratepayers, shifting much of the cost to customers.

The bill's definition of renewable biomass includes logging residues, small-diameter thinned trees, and wood or paper mill byproducts, making them credit-eligible. Whether that serves the public depends on contested views of biomass's climate and forest impacts.

Only incremental hydropower — efficiency upgrades and capacity additions at existing dams — would qualify for credits, rewarding dam owners for upgrades rather than new dams, and subject to existing environmental licensing.
